title: Operators and Expressions
subtitle: The Math and Logic Behind Your Dashboard Progress, XP and Status
description: Master all operators - arithmetic, assignment, comparison, logical, nullish, ternary - and how your dashboard calculates 20% progress, checks locked status, and handles fallbacks with ?? and ||.

blocks.text: PAGE 1: What is an Operator and Expression? Your Dashboard's Math
Hey friend! Remember variables from Lesson 2? You have xp = 120 box, completed = 2 box. Operator is a symbol that does something to those boxes. Expression is a combination that produces a value.

Example from your dashboard: (completed / TOTAL_LESSONS) * 100 - here / and * are arithmetic operators, completed and TOTAL_LESSONS are variables, whole thing (completed / TOTAL_LESSONS) * 100 is an expression that produces a value like 20.

Another example: lesson.id <= completed - here <= is comparison operator, checks if lesson id is less than or equal to completed, produces true/false boolean. Your dashboard uses this to decide if lesson shows COMPLETED badge.

Your dashboard is full of operators! Look at your HTML: Math.round((completed / TOTAL_LESSONS) * 100) uses /, *, Math.round. lesson.id <= completed uses <=. data.xp ?? data.profile?.xp ?? 0 uses ?? nullish coalescing. completed + 1 uses +.

Without operators, you cannot calculate progress, cannot check if lesson is locked, cannot add XP, cannot handle fallbacks. Operators are the verbs of JavaScript - they do actions on nouns (variables). Today you master all 6 types.

blocks.text: PAGE 2: Arithmetic Operators - Your XP and Progress Math

Arithmetic operators do math: + addition, - subtraction, * multiplication, / division, % modulo (remainder), ** exponentiation, ++ increment, -- decrement. Your dashboard uses + to add XP, / and * to calculate percent, + to get next lesson id.

Example: xp = 120, you complete lesson, xp = xp + 50 => 170. That's + operator. completed = 2, next lesson = completed + 1 => 3. That's + again. percent = (completed / total) * 100 => (2/10)*100 = 20. That's / and *.

Modulo % is tricky but useful: 10 % 3 = 1 remainder. Use case: Check if lesson id is even or odd: if (id % 2 === 0) even else odd. Or cycle through colors: colors[index % colors.length] - ensures index never goes out of bounds, wraps around.
Increment ++ adds 1: completed++ means completed = completed + 1. Decrement -- subtracts 1. Your dashboard could use completed++ when lesson completed, but uses completed = completed + 1 for clarity.

Operator precedence: * and / before + and -. So 2 + 3 * 4 = 2 + 12 = 14, not 20. Your dashboard uses parentheses to control order: (completed / TOTAL_LESSONS) * 100 - parentheses first, then * . Always use parentheses to be clear.

blocks.question: Q1: completed = 2, TOTAL_LESSONS = 10. You write let percent = completed / TOTAL_LESSONS * 100; What is percent and why parentheses (completed / TOTAL_LESSONS) * 100 vs completed / (TOTAL_LESSONS * 100) give different results? Tricky precedence!
options: First: 2/10*100 = 0.2*100 = 20% correct. Second: 2/(10*100)=2/1000=0.002=0.2% wrong! Because / and * same precedence left-to-right, so 2/10*100 = (2/10)*100 = 20, but 2/(10*100) forces 10*100 first. Your dashboard uses (completed / TOTAL_LESSONS) * 100 with parentheses to be explicit and safe
blocks.correctFeedback: Yes! Precedence left-to-right for / and *. 2/10*100 = (2/10)*100 = 20. But 2/(10*100)=2/1000=0.002. Parentheses in your dashboard (completed / TOTAL_LESSONS) * 100 makes intent clear and safe!
blocks.incorrectFeedback: / and * same precedence, evaluated left-to-right. completed / TOTAL_LESSONS * 100 = (completed/TOTAL)*100 = 20%. completed / (TOTAL*100) = completed/1000 = 0.2% - wrong! Parentheses control order, your dashboard uses (completed / TOTAL) * 100 for clarity.
blocks.reasoning: Operator precedence and parentheses - your dashboard's progress formula relies on correct order.

blocks.text: PAGE 3: Assignment Operators - Shortcuts for XP Updates
Assignment = assigns value: xp = 120. But there are shortcuts: +=, -=, *=, /=, %=. These combine assignment with arithmetic. Your dashboard could use them to make code shorter.
Instead of xp = xp + 50, you can write xp += 50 - same meaning, shorter. Instead of coins = coins + 10, coins += 10. Instead of completed = completed + 1, completed += 1 or completed++.

Your dashboard HTML uses long form: completed = completed + 1, xp = xp + 50 for clarity for beginners. But pro code uses shortcuts: xp += 50, coins += 10, completed++. Both work, shortcuts are faster to type.

Important: Difference between = and == and ===. = is assignment: xp = 120 assigns. == is loose equality check: 2 == '2' true (converts types). === is strict equality: 2 === '2' false (checks type too). Your dashboard uses === for status checks: lesson.id === completed + 1 - strict check, safer.

blocks.text: PAGE 4: Comparison Operators - Your Dashboard's Locked/Completed Logic

Comparison operators compare two values and return true/false boolean. Your dashboard uses them heavily to decide status: lesson.id <= completed means completed, lesson.id === completed + 1 means current, lesson.id > completed + 1 means locked.

Operators: == loose equality (2 == '2' true, converts types), === strict equality (2 === '2' false, checks type too - safer, your dashboard uses ===), != loose not equal, !== strict not equal, > greater than, < less than, >= greater or equal, <= less or equal.

Example: completed = 2, lesson 1: 1 <= 2 true => completed, lesson 2: 2 <= 2 true => completed, lesson 3: 3 <= 2 false, check 3 === 2+1 => 3===3 true => current, lesson 4: 4 <=2 false, 4===3 false, so else locked. That's exactly your createLessonCard logic!

Why === not ==? Because == does type coercion: '2' == 2 true, but '2' === 2 false. If completed is string '2' from localStorage and lessonId is number 3, '2' + 1 = '21' string concatenation not 3! Then 3 === '21' false. Using Number() and === prevents bugs. Your dashboard uses Number() conversion plus === for safety.

blocks.question: Q2: completed = 2 (number), lessonId = 3 (number). Check: lessonId === completed + 1? 3 === 3 true => current correct. But completed is '2' string from localStorage, lessonId = 3 number. Check: 3 === '2' + 1? '2' + 1 = '21' string, 3 === '21' false! So lesson 3 shows locked not current! How to fix like your dashboard?
options: Use == instead of === so 3 == '21' true - fixes but unsafe

Convert completed to number first: Number('2') + 1 = 3, then 3 === 3 true correct. Your dashboard does Number(completed) || 0 and Math.min/Math.max to ensure number type before comparison - prevents string concatenation bug
blocks.correctFeedback: Exactly! String + number = concatenation bug '2'+1='21'. Number('2')+1=3 correct. Your dashboard's Number(completed) || 0 and Math.min/Math.max ensures number type - pro safety!
blocks.incorrectFeedback: '2' + 1 = '21' string concatenation, not 3. 3 === '21' false, so locked incorrectly. Number('2') = 2, 2+1=3, 3===3 true current correct. Your dashboard uses Number() conversion for xp, coins, completed for this exact bug prevention.
blocks.reasoning: String from storage + number = concatenation bug - critical bug that breaks status logic - your dashboard fixes with Number().

blocks.text: PAGE 5: Logical Operators - &&, ||, ! - Your Dashboard's Auth and Fallbacks

Logical operators work with booleans: && AND, || OR, ! NOT. Your dashboard uses them everywhere: if (document.referrer && document.referrer.includes(location.origin)) - && means both conditions must be true. if (!user) - ! means NOT, if NOT user then redirect to login.

&& AND: true && true = true, true && false = false, false && anything = false. Use case: Check multiple conditions: if (isLoggedIn && completed >= 2) - both must be true to start lesson 3. Your back button: referrer exists AND referrer includes origin - both true to do history.back().

|| OR: true || false = true, false || false = false, true || anything = true. Use case: Fallbacks: Number(data.xp || 0) - if data.xp exists use it, else 0. Your dashboard: data.xp ?? data.profile?.xp ?? 0 - tries first, if null/undefined tries second, else 0. || similar but ?? better for 0.

! NOT: !true = false, !false = true, !null = true, !0 = true, !'hello' = false. Your dashboard: if (!user) redirect - if user is null, !null = true, so redirect. If user exists, !user = false, don't redirect. ! flips boolean.

Short-circuit: && and || don't evaluate second part if first decides result. true || anything = true without checking second, false && anything = false without checking second. Your dashboard: document.referrer && document.referrer.includes(...) - if referrer is empty string '', '' && ... short-circuits false, doesn't call includes on empty, prevents error. Safe pattern!

blocks.question: Q3: Your dashboard back button code: if (document.referrer && document.referrer.includes(location.origin)) { history.back() } else { go to menu.html }. referrer = '' empty string. What happens with && short-circuit and why is && used not just includes?
options: Calls includes on empty string and errors

Short-circuit: '' is falsy, so '' && anything = false without evaluating second part, so includes not called, prevents error calling includes on empty/null. If you did only referrer.includes without checking referrer exists first, and referrer is null, null.includes would throw TypeError: Cannot read property includes of null
blocks.correctFeedback: Yes! && short-circuit prevents error. If referrer is null/empty, first part falsy, second part not evaluated, no error. Without && check, null.includes would crash. Your dashboard's && pattern is safe pro pattern!
blocks.incorrectFeedback: '' && includes short-circuits false, includes not called. null && includes also short-circuits. Without &&, if referrer null, null.includes() throws TypeError. && ensures referrer exists before calling includes - safe!
blocks.reasoning: Short-circuit with && prevents errors when first value might be null/empty - your dashboard's back button safety pattern.

blocks.text: PAGE 6: Nullish Coalescing ?? and Optional Chaining ?. - Your Dashboard's Modern Safety

?? is nullish coalescing: returns right side only if left is null or undefined, keeps 0 and '' and false. Your dashboard: data.xp ?? data.profile?.xp ?? 0 - if data.xp is null/undefined, try data.profile?.xp, if that null/undefined, use 0. If data.xp is 0, keeps 0 not fallback - important because 0 XP is valid!

?. is optional chaining: data.profile?.xp means if data.profile exists, get xp, if data.profile is null/undefined, return undefined instead of error. Your dashboard: data.profile?.xp - if profile doesn't exist, don't throw error, return undefined, then ?? tries next fallback. Without ?., data.profile.xp would throw TypeError if profile null.

Difference || vs ??: || falls back for any falsy (0, '', false, null, undefined), ?? falls back only for null/undefined, keeps 0, '', false. For XP, 0 is valid XP, should keep 0 not fallback to 10, so ?? better. Your dashboard uses ?? for xp and ?. for safe property access.

Your exact dashboard code: const xp = Number(data.xp ?? data.profile?.xp ?? 0); - tries data.xp, if null/undefined tries data.profile?.xp (safe access), if that null/undefined uses 0, then Number() converts to number. This handles all cases: Firebase has xp directly, or in profile sub-object, or no xp at all.

blocks.question: Q4: User has 0 XP (new user). You have let xp = data.xp || 10; and let xp2 = data.xp ?? 10; data.xp = 0. What are xp and xp2? Why your dashboard uses ?? for XP not ||? Very tricky close options!
options: xp = 10, xp2 = 0 - because || treats 0 as falsy so fallback to 10, losing valid 0 XP, shows 10 XP incorrectly. ?? only falls back for null/undefined, keeps 0 as valid XP. Your dashboard uses ?? to keep 0 XP for new users, not incorrectly show 10 XP
blocks.correctFeedback: Perfect! 0 XP is valid for new user, should show 0 not 10. || would incorrectly show 10, ?? correctly keeps 0. Your dashboard's ?? is correct for XP, coins, completed where 0 is valid!
blocks.incorrectFeedback: 0 || 10 = 10 because 0 falsy, fallback. 0 ?? 10 = 0 because 0 not null/undefined, keep. For XP, 0 valid, should keep 0 not 10, so ?? correct. Your dashboard: data.xp ?? ... ?? 0 keeps 0 XP correctly.
blocks.reasoning: || vs ?? with 0 - critical for XP where 0 is valid value - your dashboard uses ?? correctly to preserve 0.

blocks.text: PAGE 7: Ternary Operator - Your Dashboard's Short if/else

Ternary operator is short if/else: condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse. Your dashboard could use it for status badge text: status === 'completed' ? 'Completed' : status === 'current' ? 'Current' : 'Locked' - nested ternary for 3 conditions.

Example: let badge = isCompleted ? 'Completed' : 'Locked' - if isCompleted true, badge = 'Completed', else 'Locked'. Shorter than if/else. Your dashboard uses if/else for statusHTML for clarity, but ternary is shorter for simple cases.
Precedence: Ternary has lower precedence than || and &&, so use parentheses. Example: let xp = data.xp ?? 0; let text = xp > 0 ? `${xp} XP` : 'No XP' - if xp >0 show XP, else No XP.

blocks.question: Q5: You have if (user && user.xp && user.xp >= 100) { show premium }. user = {xp: 0}. What happens? 0 is falsy, so user.xp is falsy, condition false, premium not shown even though user exists with 0 XP. How to fix for XP where 0 valid? Tricky!
options: Keep user.xp check - 0 XP means no premium correct

Use user && user.xp !== null && user.xp !== undefined && user.xp >= 100 - check null/undefined explicitly, not falsy, so 0 XP still checked for >=100 (0>=100 false, so no premium, but for different reason). Or use user?.xp ?? 0 >=100 with optional chaining and nullish. The bug is using truthy check for XP where 0 valid but falsy
blocks.correctFeedback: Yes! user.xp as condition fails for 0 XP because 0 falsy. Need explicit null/undefined check: user.xp !== null && user.xp !== undefined, or user?.xp ?? 0, then >=100. 0 XP should be checked for >=100, not treated as missing!
blocks.incorrectFeedback: user.xp where xp=0 is falsy, so user.xp && ... short-circuits false, premium not shown. But reason wrong - should check xp exists (not null/undefined) not truthy. Fix: user?.xp !== null && user?.xp !== undefined && user.xp >=100 or (user?.xp ?? 0) >=100. 0 valid value should be checked.
blocks.reasoning: Falsy 0 bug with && - user.xp 0 is valid but falsy, breaks condition - need explicit null check not truthy check.

blocks.text: PAGE 10: Summary & Tricky Final Questions

You mastered all operators: Arithmetic + - * / % ** ++ -- for XP and progress math, Assignment = += -= *= /= for shortcuts, Comparison == === != !== > < >= <= for status logic with === strict safer than ==, Logical && || ! for auth and fallbacks with short-circuit safety, Nullish ?? keeps 0 but falls back for null/undefined, Optional chaining ?. prevents errors, Ternary ? : short if/else.

blocks.question: Q6: You have let a = 0; let b = ''; let c = null; let d = undefined; Which are falsy and which nullish? And what does if (a || b || c || d || 10) give? Tricky!
options: a=0 falsy not nullish, b='' falsy not nullish, c=null falsy and nullish, d=undefined falsy and nullish. a||b||c||d||10 = 10 because all falsy, so fallback 10. a??b??c??d??10 = 0 because a=0 not nullish, so keeps 0. Difference: || checks falsy, ?? checks null/undefined only
blocks.correctFeedback: Perfect! Falsy: 0, '', false, null, undefined, NaN. Nullish: only null, undefined. 0 and '' are falsy but not nullish - important difference! Your dashboard uses ?? to keep 0 and '' valid.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Falsy = 0, '', false, null, undefined, NaN are false in if(). Nullish = only null, undefined. So 0 and '' are falsy but NOT nullish. || falls back for falsy, ?? only for nullish. For XP 0 valid, need ?? not ||.
blocks.reasoning: Falsy vs nullish distinction - 0 and '' are falsy but not nullish - critical for || vs ?? choice.

blocks.question: Q7: completed = 2, you write if (completed = 3) { console.log('Completed 3') } vs if (completed === 3). First uses = assignment, second === comparison. What happens? Common bug!
options: First: completed = 3 assigns 3 to completed, expression value is 3 which is truthy, so if (3) true, logs, AND completed now 3 - bug! Assignment in if changes variable accidentally. Second: completed === 3 checks if completed equals 3, 2===3 false, doesn't log, completed stays 2 - correct check. Never use = in if condition, use === for comparison
blocks.correctFeedback: Yes! = in if is assignment bug, changes variable! === is comparison. Your dashboard uses === for status checks, not = . Common typo bug - if (completed = 3) instead of if (completed === 3) accidentally changes completed to 3!
blocks.incorrectFeedback: if (completed = 3) assigns 3 to completed, evaluates to 3 truthy, logs, and completed becomes 3 - bug! if (completed === 3) compares, 2===3 false, doesn't log, completed stays 2. = assignment, === comparison - never mix in if!
blocks.reasoning: = vs === in if condition - assignment bug changes variable - your dashboard uses === correctly for status checks.
